headline: Nashville Songwriter Finds Calling Rescuing Foxes From Mange Epidemic
meta_description: A 78-year-old country music veteran has logged thousands of volunteer hours rescuing foxes suffering from a Tennessee mange epidemic, turning social media into…
summary_short: Jerry Vandiver, whose songs were recorded by Tim McGraw, now spends his nights trapping and rescuing foxes afflicted with mange across Nashville.
body:
At 78 years old, Jerry Vandiver has found a second calling that matters more to him than his first. The Nashville singer-songwriter, whose compositions have been recorded by country stars including Tim McGraw, has spent the last seven years volunteering thousands of hours to rescue red foxes suffering from a devastating mange epidemic sweeping Tennessee. What started as posts on his performing artist Facebook page—before-and-after videos of rescued foxes—has grown his following from 325 to 5,000 people, all watching a man at an age most would consider retirement years wake at any hour to retrieve traps from the woods and drive foxes half an hour to Walden's Puddle Animal Rescue.

Mange, caused by skin mites, is treatable but often fatal in wild foxes due to secondary infections and rapid spread through family groups called "leashes." The disease is particularly severe in Nashville's suburbs, where suburban development has forced fox families to overlap territories, accelerating transmission. In August alone, Vandiver logged 234 volunteer hours. By September 2025, Walden's Puddle had already rehabilitated 60 red foxes—surpassing their entire 2024 total of 44.

Vandiver monitors trail cameras around his house and responds to concerned citizens who contact him on Facebook with sightings of afflicted foxes. "I'm not the hero, I'm just the ambulance driver," he told the Tennessean. "Mange is treatable. If we can catch them, they can have a healthy, happy life." A staff member at Walden's Puddle noted that Vandiver puts "foxes before himself, always"—a testament to dedication that transforms an aging musician into something far more vital: a lifeline for creatures most people never notice until disease makes them impossible to ignore.
